title: Cron and Automation
subtitle: crontab syntax, scheduling tasks, @daily/@weekly, logging cron output
author: KERNAL Team

content.text: Cron is the classic Unix job scheduler — a background daemon that runs commands at a specific time or interval. Every user has their own crontab (cron table), a file listing what to run and when. It is built into every Linux distribution and macOS.

content.code:
# Edit your crontab (opens in $EDITOR)
crontab -e

# List current crontab entries
crontab -l

# Remove your entire crontab (careful!)
crontab -r

# Edit crontab for a specific user (root only)
crontab -u alice -e

# View cron logs (Ubuntu/Debian)
grep CRON /var/log/syslog

# View cron logs (macOS)
log show --predicate 'process == "cron"' --last 1h

# Format:
# ┌─────────── minute       (0-59)
# │ ┌───────── hour         (0-23)
# │ │ ┌─────── day of month (1-31)
# │ │ │ ┌───── month        (1-12)
# │ │ │ │ ┌─── day of week  (0-7, 0 and 7 = Sunday)
# │ │ │ │ │
# * * * * *  command to run

# Special values:
# *   = every (every minute, every hour, etc.)
# ,   = list  (1,5,10 = at 1, 5, and 10)
# -   = range (1-5 = 1 through 5)
# /   = step  (*/15 = every 15 minutes)

# Examples:
# Run at 2:30am every day:
30 2 * * * /home/alice/backup.sh

# Run every 15 minutes:
*/15 * * * * /usr/bin/check_health.sh

# Run at 9am Monday through Friday:
0 9 * * 1-5 /home/alice/send_report.sh

# Run at midnight on the 1st of every month:
0 0 1 * * /home/alice/monthly_cleanup.sh

# Run every hour:
0 * * * * /home/alice/sync.sh

# By default, cron emails output to the user (often silently discarded)
# Always redirect output explicitly:

# Redirect both stdout and stderr to a log file
30 2 * * * /home/alice/backup.sh >> /home/alice/logs/backup.log 2>&1

# Discard all output (use only when you're sure the script works)
30 2 * * * /home/alice/backup.sh > /dev/null 2>&1

# Log with timestamps using tee
30 2 * * * /home/alice/backup.sh 2>&1 | tee -a /home/alice/logs/backup.log

# Important: cron runs with a minimal PATH (/usr/bin:/bin)
# If your script uses tools like node, python, git — use FULL paths
# or set PATH at the top of your crontab:
PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/home/alice/.local/bin
30 2 * * * backup.sh  # now can find node, git, etc.

# Or use full path inside the script:
/usr/local/bin/node /home/alice/app/sync.js

# Tip: always test the script manually first before scheduling it:
bash /home/alice/backup.sh

content.text: Use full paths for commands in crontab entries. Cron runs with a very minimal PATH — commands like node, python3, or git that work in your terminal won't be found by cron unless you specify their full path (e.g., /usr/local/bin/node) or set a PATH= variable at the top of the crontab file.

questions.question: You want to run /home/alice/backup.sh every day at 3:30am. Which crontab entry is correct?
questions.explanation: Cron fields are: minute hour day month weekday. So 30 3 * * * means minute 30, hour 3, every day of the month, every month, every day of the week — i.e., 3:30am daily. Option B reverses minute and hour (would run at 3am on the 30th minute of every hour). @daily always runs at midnight and doesn't take a time argument.

faq.q: My cron job works when I run the script manually but not as a cron job. Why?
faq.a: Cron runs with a minimal environment: no .bashrc, no .profile, and a very limited PATH. Fixes: (1) Use full absolute paths for all commands. (2) Add PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin and any other directories at the top of your crontab. (3) Source your profile at the start of the script: source /home/user/.bashrc. Always redirect output to a log file to see what error cron is reporting.

faq.q: What is the difference between cron and systemd timers?
faq.a: systemd timers are the modern Linux alternative. They support: missed-run catchup (runs a job even if the system was off at the scheduled time), per-job logging in the systemd journal (journalctl -u mytimer.timer), better error handling, and dependency management. For new Linux services, prefer systemd timers. For macOS, use launchd plist files (or a modern wrapper like launchd-crontab). Cron is still widely used for its simplicity and cross-platform availability.

examples: 0 2 * * * pg_dump myapp | gzip > /backups/myapp-$(date +%Y%m%d).sql.gz — automated nightly database backup
@reboot sleep 10 && /home/deploy/app/start.sh — auto-start a custom app after every system reboot, with a 10s delay for networking to initialize
